overview: Zambia’s regional history includes extraordinary traces of early woodworking and the ordinary skills of preparing and sharing food. Archaeological finds and local accounts reveal different kinds of knowledge, separated by immense stretches of time.

periods.title: Northern Rhodesia under company administration
periods.summary: The first map record begins when the territory was called Northern Rhodesia. The British South Africa Company administered it before the transfer to direct British colonial administration in 1924. The modern name on the map is a later label.

periods.title: Direct British colonial administration
periods.summary: Administration passed to the British Colonial Office in 1924. The Legislative Council first met in Livingstone on 23 May that year. Colonial institutions changed over time; this was still decades before independence.

periods.title: Federation and its dissolution
periods.summary: In 1953, Northern Rhodesia joined Southern Rhodesia and Nyasaland in a federation opposed by African nationalist leaders. The federation collapsed in 1963. Northern Rhodesia’s independence followed in 1964, rather than automatically arriving with the federation’s end.

periods.title: The independent republic
periods.summary: Zambia became independent on 24 October 1964. Its parliamentary institutions had their colonial beginnings in 1924. This ended British rule while opening new debates over how the republic would be governed.

periods.title: The move to one-party government
periods.summary: The 2005 Constitution Review Commission dates the broad one-party period from 1972. The 1973 constitution formalised that system under UNIP. Reforms in December 1990 reopened the way to multiparty elections, which followed in 1991.

periods.title: Multiparty elections return
periods.summary: The Movement for Multi-party Democracy won the presidential and parliamentary elections of 31 October 1991, and UNIP became the opposition. This was a change of government within Zambia, rather than the creation of a new country.

periods.title: Music passed to new generations
periods.summary: Kalela dance joined UNESCO’s Representative List in 2022. Its performers preserve and renew skills through public participation, singing and drumming, with some groups also organising lessons for new musicians.

sections.title: Woodworking in the very distant past

items.text: Excavations at Kalambo Falls in 2019 uncovered two logs joined through a deliberately shaped notch. Their waterlogged deposits were dated to roughly 476,000 years ago, with a margin of uncertainty. Researchers interpret them as parts of a wooden construction. A platform, walkway or foundation is possible; the find is not a complete house with a known floor plan.

The wet conditions at Kalambo helped wood survive where it would usually decay. The researchers also had to protect it after excavation. They used photographs and digital models to examine the shaping marks while keeping the pieces submerged. Studying an ancient wooden object could mean photographing it in a bath, rather than simply drying it and putting it on a shelf.

sections.title: A game board with room for thought

items.text: A wooden cisolwa board in the British Museum has four rows of eight holes. The catalogue attributes it to Lala makers in Zambia and dates it approximately between 1957 and 1972. It is more than a metre wide. This game took up rather more space than a phone screen. The object preserves a material trace of play, even though its catalogue does not explain every move.

sections.title: Making dinner could be a group project

items.text: Sociologist Mwizenge Tembo describes preparing maize meal with help from children, relatives and neighbours. After kernels were removed from the cobs, women and girls pounded the maize, sometimes accompanying the work with songs. His account draws on fieldwork in 1980, 1985 and 1993, especially around eastern Zambia. It makes the labour behind a meal visible, alongside the cooperation involved.

Tembo explains how nshima, a thick porridge, is eaten with another dish that might contain vegetables, beans, meat or fish. Diners shape a small portion in one hand and dip it into the accompanying dish. Conversation and hospitality form part of his account too. The meal is a social occasion as well as a way to satisfy hunger.

A 2016 Bioversity International project in the Barotse Floodplain brought people together in cooking groups. Its description records recipe sharing, cookbooks and seasonal food calendars, connecting available ingredients with family meals. The calendar helped make a practical question visible: what food is available at this time of year? This example concerns the participating communities, rather than one menu followed across Zambia.

sections.title: Learn the dance by joining in

items.text: Kalela developed in colonial-era Luapula and was taken up by mine workers. UNESCO describes dancers moving in two or three lines, singing as they go forwards and backwards around central drums. Lead singers and dancers help guide the group. The performance depends on people coordinating movement, rhythm and voice, making it both skilled work and a shared occasion.

Kalela skills are passed on through songs, poetry, watching and participation. Some groups also organise lessons with experienced drummers when they need new musicians. Performances belong to occasions ranging from weddings to public celebrations and funerals. There is more than one way to learn: sometimes a lesson has a teacher at the front, and sometimes it has a drumbeat in the middle.

sections.title: Building a university, then training teachers

items.text: The University of Zambia began its first academic session at Lusaka’s Ridgeway Campus on 17 March 1966. That first day followed a commission, planning, legal establishment and recruitment of staff. The university’s own history separates the start of classes from the later July ceremonies. A school’s beginning can have several important dates, depending on whether we mean its paperwork, its buildings or its students.

The School of Education opened in April 1966 with forty-two graduates studying for a postgraduate teaching certificate. By 1969 its programmes also included training for primary teachers and courses in library studies. Preparing people to teach, and people to organise books and information, helped extend the work of learning beyond the university’s own classrooms.

ending.text: British rule ended on 24 October 1964, when Northern Rhodesia became independent as Zambia. The republic continued through later changes in its political system, including the return to multiparty elections in 1991. The earlier map intervals are not dates when Zambian communities disappeared.
